posts.author: Stereofan
posts.content_md: Is it possible to calculate a given hologram from a stereoscopic (two-photo) set of images I'm wondering how to reconstruct a holographic image from multiple perspective shots, if it is.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
While I don't know if any researchers are doing it now, I think it's only a matter of time and computer resources before it happens.

Several researchers in the computer graphics field have developed methods to generate full 3D computer models based off multiple shots of a city and from that kind of data and algorithms we aren't far from creating a hologram. The computer power needed to create the hologram is pretty significant but is well within the possible.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: I'm pretty certain it's being done. Using 2 perspective views and generating intermediate views from them by computer. At a show once, I saw a company that was taking two perspective views and having a milling machine cut out a bust of the person photographed. I've also heard of other holographers doing that for making stereograms but can't remember who it was.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
Even with cheap morphing software you can get a pretty good data set from two images. This is not as computer intensive as trying to calculate the depth of each point.

[http://www.morpheussoftware.net/](http://www.morpheussoftware.net/)

With a LCD stereogram set up this wold not be all that hard.If you just want to see it work make a data set and have Liti shoot the hologram for you, they have a stock service for converting footage into holograms.

posts.author: Kaveh
posts.content_md: A company called [Digimask](http://www.digimask.com/) can do it from *one* photo! Mind you, the software assumes a full frontal photo of a human face.

posts.author: Stereofan
posts.content_md:
Alright, let me be clearer here, since there seems to be some topic confusion -- I'm not interested in 3d reconstruction of views intermediate to multiple perspectives; that's a VIRTUAL reconstruction (actually, I AM interested in this, but it's for another, separate project: one where I project feedback through an hmd like Icuiti or the z800 to the user of a fly-around).

 What I am interested in is taking a stereopair and calculating the interferometric equivalent, perhaps using some kind of fourier transform, so that the holographic equivalent of the stereoimage can be recorded, even if in a narrowly viewed format from a narrow angle of view. It would be nice to know the limitations and advantages of such transforms (stereomovie transformation via multiplex method,eg ???).

 Mostly, though, I'm trying to think about how to contribute to the growth and utility of holography as a discipline. If stereography and holography were made interconvertible, it would make for some rather interesting exercises, especially as there is so much stereography to work with.

posts.author: Stereofan
posts.content_md: PS thanks for the tip on Liti, colin.

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md: Maybe you are thinking of a holographic autostereogram? Essentially you can make a very simple multiplex hologram that combines left and right images of a stereogram so that it can be viewed without special glasses and with left and right eyes seeing the proper views - but only when viewed directly facing the hologram. Saxby in "Practical Holography" 3rd ed. has a short description of the method.

posts.author: Stereofan
posts.content_md:
Yes, something like that. I have read Frank DeFreitas work, and it seems he has taken down the work he did on the technical aspects of beamforming/filtration as well as the offer for an inexpensive diode kit. This is a shame as I quite enjoyed and valued that specific part of the site above the rest of the stuff.

 It's possible that if I have understood it correctly -- that the autostereoscopic holography is a series of stereogram shot with interference patterns originating from object beams' transmittance through the stereogram negatives -- that the holoportrait suggestion may be what I am interested in, however, if so, the discussion concerning how to achieve a small portion of what I suggest still leaves the rest "out in the cold", ie, eg, if the stereoscopic capture will yield a narrowly deep slice-of-perspective as opposed to a whole hologram's "window on the world" viewpoint what limitations are there to the narrow but deep perspective? I gather repeated perspective change over a range of perspective can add to the domain, in some limited fashion. I don't know enough of this though to fruitfully speculate.

 What would be especially nice would be to use multiple stereopairs spaced apart by stereotrajectory/ies (coining new terms now?) in which morphing software can generate the intermediate steps between pairs.

This would allow one trajectory view to result in the (relatively) smooth? change of one object into another. It might be repeated with different stereopairs that still had enough similarities at a converging point to allow for different motion perspective "transforms" while at the same time preserving enough object integrity to do startling things.

 Again, my objective is to think of how to broaden the existing array of experimental techniques/media/subject matter. Try wrapping your head around that and see what happens.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: It would be a one day project to generate the data and submit it to Liti for printing. You could see your idea in hand in less than a week and for less than $800 in full color.
